items.title: 16.7 Tests for identification of basic radicals

source_refs.note: Topic 16.7 with Quick Check 16.4, printed pages 345-347. The print labels both iron tests 'f)' and describes the Fe2+ precipitate with ammonia as 'white gelatinous'. The exercise (pages 348-349) is not reproduced.

blocks.text: For each cation (basic radical) about 4 g of the solid sample is dissolved in about 10 cm3 of distilled water and the solution divided into two parts: one part is tested with NaOH solution and the other with aqueous ammonia.

blocks.caption: Cation tests with NaOH(aq) and NH3(aq)
rows: warm gently: ammonia gas with a distinct smell, turns moist red litmus blue
white precipitate, does not dissolve in excess NaOH
only a slight turbidity, or no precipitate
green precipitate, turns into a green solution in excess NaOH
green precipitate, insoluble in excess ammonia
green precipitate, turns orange-brown after some time
white gelatinous precipitate of Fe(OH)2 that quickly oxidises to red-brown Fe(OH)3
white precipitate, soluble in excess NaOH
white precipitate, dissolves in excess ammonia

blocks.title: Hydroxide precipitates
blocks.text: Al3+ + 3OH- -> Al(OH)3 white ppt; NH4+ + OH- -> NH3 + H2O; Ca2+ + 2OH- -> Ca(OH)2 white ppt; Cr3+ + 3OH- -> Cr(OH)3 green ppt; Cu2+ + 2OH- -> Cu(OH)2 blue ppt; Fe2+ + 2OH- -> Fe(OH)2 green ppt; Fe3+ + 3OH- -> Fe(OH)3 orange-brown ppt; Zn2+ + 2OH- -> Zn(OH)2 white ppt

blocks.alt: Three test tubes: pale blue [Cu(H2O)6]2+; with a small amount of ammonia a blue precipitate [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2] (ammonia acting as a base); with an excess of ammonia a deep blue solution [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (ligand exchange reaction).
blocks.caption: Copper(II) ions with a small amount and an excess of ammonia (original drawing after the figure printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: What is the lake test, how is the ammonium ion indicated, how are Fe2+ and Fe3+ distinguished, and what happens when aqueous ammonia is added to Cu2+ in limited and in excess amounts?
